title: 22. Interview: CDN & Content Delivery
summary: Interview Q&A for CDN & Content Delivery — 15 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 15 CDN & Content Delivery interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: 15 Interview Questions with Answers
sections.body:
### Q1: What is a CDN and how does it work?

**Answer:** CDN is a network of geographically distributed servers that cache content close to users. DNS routes requests to nearest edge server (PoP). If content is cached (HIT), served from edge (low latency). If MISS, fetched from origin, cached at edge, then served. Benefits: lower latency, reduced origin load, DDoS protection, handles traffic spikes.

### Q2: Push CDN vs Pull CDN?

**Answer:** **Push**: You upload content to CDN proactively. Full control, no cache misses on first request. Good for: predictable, static content. **Pull**: CDN fetches from origin on first request, then caches. Simpler setup, auto-manages cache. Good for: dynamic sites, large content catalogs. Most production systems use Pull with cache warming for popular content.

### Q3: How do you handle cache invalidation in a CDN?

**Answer:** (1) **TTL**: Set max-age, content expires automatically. (2) **Purge API**: Explicitly invalidate URLs. (3) **Versioned URLs**: `/app.v2.js` — new URL = guaranteed fresh. (4) **Surrogate keys/tags**: Tag content, purge by tag. (5) **stale-while-revalidate**: Serve stale, update in background. Best practice: version static assets (immutable cache), short TTL for HTML, purge API for urgent changes.

### Q4: How would you design a system for serving images at scale?

**Answer:** Architecture: Upload → S3 (original) → Processing queue → Generate variants (thumbnail, medium, HD) → Store variants → CDN. On-request transformation: URL params define size/format → CDN edge transforms → cache result. Use WebP/AVIF for modern browsers (Accept header). Pre-signed URLs for upload. Content-hash URLs for cache busting. Progressive JPEG for perceived performance.

### Q5: What is cache warming?

**Answer:** Proactively loading content into CDN cache before users request it. Used after: new deployment, cache flush, new edge server added. Approach: identify top-N most requested URLs (from analytics), make requests to populate cache. Benefits: avoid cache stampede, consistent performance. Can run as scheduled job or triggered by deployment pipeline.

### Q6: How does DNS-based routing work for CDNs?

**Answer:** User requests `cdn.example.com`. CDN's authoritative DNS server checks user's resolver IP → determines geographic region → returns IP of nearest edge. Techniques: (1) **GeoDNS** — route by geography. (2) **Latency-based** — route by measured latency. (3) **Anycast** — same IP announced from multiple locations, BGP routes to nearest. Anycast is most common for large CDNs (Cloudflare uses it).

### Q7: How do you handle dynamic content with CDN?

**Answer:** (1) **Edge computing** (Cloudflare Workers) — run code at edge, (2) **Short TTL** — cache for seconds, not hours, (3) **stale-while-revalidate** — serve cached, update async, (4) **Vary header** — cache different versions (by cookie, user-agent), (5) **ESI (Edge Side Includes)** — cache page fragments separately, (6) **Microcaching** — cache for 1-5 seconds (handles traffic spikes).

### Q8: Explain pre-signed URLs.

**Answer:** Pre-signed URL gives temporary, limited access to a private resource. Server generates URL with: resource path, expiration time, permissions, HMAC signature. Client uses URL directly (no auth needed). Use cases: (1) Direct upload to S3 (server never handles file), (2) Time-limited download links, (3) Sharing private content. Security: URL expires, signature prevents tampering, one-time use optional.

### Q9: How would you design a video streaming system?

**Answer:** (1) **Upload** → Transcode into multiple bitrates (240p to 4K), (2) **Segment** → Split into small chunks (2-10 seconds each), (3) **Manifest** → HLS/DASH manifest lists available qualities and segments, (4) **CDN** → Distribute segments to edge servers, (5) **Player** → Adaptive bitrate streaming (switches quality based on bandwidth). Netflix uses Open Connect (own CDN). YouTube uses Google's global CDN.

### Q10: What is the thundering herd problem and how does CDN handle it?

**Answer:** When cache expires, many concurrent requests all miss cache and hit origin simultaneously. Solutions: (1) **Request coalescing** — CDN groups concurrent misses into single origin request, (2) **Stale-while-revalidate** — serve stale while one request updates, (3) **Lock/semaphore** — only one request fetches, others wait, (4) **Pre-warm** — refresh cache before expiry. Most CDNs implement request coalescing automatically.

### Q11: How do you implement cache busting?

**Answer:** (1) **Content hash in filename**: `app.a1b2c3.js` — changes when content changes. Best practice, immutable cache forever. (2) **Query string version**: `app.js?v=123` — some CDNs don't cache query strings. (3) **Path version**: `/v2/app.js`. Build tools (Webpack, Vite) automate content hashing. HTML references hashed assets. HTML itself uses short TTL.

### Q12: Compare CloudFront, Cloudflare, and Akamai.

**Answer:** **CloudFront**: AWS native, integrates with S3/Lambda@Edge, pay-per-use, good for AWS shops. **Cloudflare**: Global anycast, free tier, Workers (edge compute), DDoS protection built-in, easy setup. **Akamai**: Largest CDN, enterprise focus, best for media streaming, most PoPs worldwide, expensive. Choose: Cloudflare for simplicity, CloudFront for AWS, Akamai for enterprise/media.

### Q13: How does a CDN help with DDoS protection?

**Answer:** (1) **Absorb traffic** — CDN has massive bandwidth across many PoPs, (2) **Distribute attack** — anycast spreads traffic across edges, (3) **Rate limiting** — edge-level rate limiting per IP, (4) **WAF** — block malicious requests at edge, (5) **Bot detection** — JavaScript challenges, CAPTCHA, (6) **Origin shield** — CDN handles traffic, origin gets minimal requests. Cloudflare handles 100+ Tbps attacks.

### Q14: What are Edge Functions/Workers?

**Answer:** Serverless functions that run at CDN edge locations. Execute code close to users with sub-millisecond cold start. Use cases: (1) A/B testing (route at edge), (2) Authentication (verify JWT at edge), (3) API response transformation, (4) Personalization, (5) Rate limiting. Platforms: Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda@Edge, Vercel Edge Functions. Run in V8 isolates (not containers) for fast startup.

### Q15: Design a global content distribution system for Netflix.

**Answer:** Netflix uses **Open Connect**: (1) Content ingested → encoded into 100+ formats per title (device-specific), (2) Overnight, push popular content to ISP-embedded servers (Open Connect Appliances), (3) DNS routes user to nearest OCA, (4) Adaptive streaming: client requests manifest, downloads segments from nearest OCA, (5) Cache hierarchy: ISP OCA → regional hub → origin (S3), (6) Popularity-based caching: hot titles cached everywhere, niche titles at regional hubs only.

**Next Chapter: [Data Engineering →](../09_Data_Engineering/01_Data_Pipelines.md)**
